quote: It's 20, but one's broken. So let's call it nineteen, two hundred and sixty five kilowatt panels.
stewart_read: This is a strong lead-quality signal — an existing system that is broken/undersized and a customer who has already done the math herself. This is not a standard schema section (the schema's enthusiasm examples focus on trees/EV/pool-type signals), but it functions the same way: it materially raises this lead's value and warrants an anchor-back from the rep.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to verbally reflect this back ('so you've already identified the exact gap — that's exactly what our design team needs') to build the customer's sense that this call is moving her problem forward, not just re-collecting data she already has.

quote: I'm looking to add on to that system. That system is not properly sized for this house.
stewart_read: This is a distinct, high-value signal separate from the battery-backup mention: the customer is explicitly requesting a system expansion due to undersizing, which is core Ion business but sits in the schema's acknowledged TBD gap (battery_storage_inquiry / system-expansion cross-sell isn't yet codified). The rep captures the fact procedurally but never reflects it back as a value point.
coaching_implication: Manager should note this as a real-world example to bring to Kenny for populating the battery_storage_inquiry / expansion cross-sell catalog — this call is evidence the pattern exists and isn't rare.

quote: Oh, what I'm surprised you didn't get this information. I've provided all of this information.
stewart_read: Customer directly names a process friction (repeated data requests) — this maps to the schema's C6 list of TBD/emerging protocols (excessive_contact_complaint is listed as a placeholder, not a populated protocol), so this should be read as an emerging pattern worth flagging to Kenny rather than a documented procedure the rep violated.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have had no way to see prior-submitted data and the redundancy is a systems/CRM gap rather than a rep failure.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to lead with acknowledgment when a customer flags redundancy ('you're right, let me not make you repeat that') rather than a neutral technical explanation, regardless of whether the systems gap is the rep's fault.

quote: No. They're not accepting that metering. I know that. Yeah.
stewart_read: The customer already knew about the WASCO net-metering freeze before the rep found it. Had the rep checked or asked about utility program status earlier in the utility_company verify step (02:17), this could have surfaced sooner and avoided walking the customer through the full bill-collection discussion before hitting the wall.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may not have had access to utility-status information until later in their process/tooling, making the sequencing unavoidable rather than a rep error.
coaching_implication: Discuss with the rep whether utility-eligibility checks can be moved earlier in the call flow (right after utility name is captured) to avoid extended qualification effort on a likely-DQ'd utility.

quote: Apparently, we're not able to work with WASCO, because as of right now, their the utility company is not accepting any solar applications and does not have any plans to reopen their solar program at the at the moment.
stewart_read: This isn't a clean hard DQ per the schema's dq_rules list — it's a utility-program-availability issue the rep is uncertain about ('this looks like it was updated as of, a year ago'), so the rep's decision to defer rather than DQ outright is the more defensible read given the ambiguity.
alternative_hypothesis: A stricter reading would call this a dq outcome since the rep effectively told the customer Ion cannot proceed; but the rep's own words treat it as provisional pending design-team confirmation.
coaching_implication: Manager should confirm with Kenny whether WASCO status is verified in real time or if reps are working from stale data — this call is evidence the eligibility check itself may need refreshing.

quote: No. I again, I don't wanna be wasting your time if it's not gonna be, if we're not gonna be able to help you. So I don't wanna have you grab all that for me.
stewart_read: The call ends with no locked callback time, no bill collected, and no specific next step other than a vague promise to check with the design team. There is no 'is that fair' handshake or specific time commitment.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the DQ ambiguity, deferring bill collection is reasonable — the reactive failure is not in withholding the bill ask, but in failing to give the customer any concrete timeframe for the callback.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to always attach a specific timeframe to a callback promise ('I'll call you back by Thursday') even when the outcome is uncertain, so the customer isn't left with an open-ended non-commitment.
